By Sir ROBERT DONALD, GB.

HERE is a coming issue which cannot be
ignored—the extent to. which broad
casting will interfere with the progress. of
the Press, or change its character. At thi
of ‘development, radio is anally
father than a rival. It is a supplementary
service, not an alternative. At fisst, wireless
regarded as supplementary
Now. it is looked upon as a serious,
Radio is a cheap universal
information, news, education, and. enter:
tainment service which is delivered into the
homes of millions and can be broadcast to
Inany more millions of Tisteners,

‘Already newspapers are” jealous of the
potential competitor. ‘The combined Press
Organizations in Great Britain presented a
tase to the recent Broadcasting Committee
to prove why the circulation of news. by
radio should be restricted to. the present
Iimits, which are that the service is sold: to
the Broadcasting Committee by. all the
ascociated news agencies for issue at a time
which suits. the newspapers and that all
direct broadcasting should be confined to

hes without curtailment or description
Or to. the bare results of sporting and other
events

Hitherto, England has occupied a middle
Position in the radio world’ as between
Europe and Amierica. In » Continental
‘countries Governments liave concerned theim-
selves more directly with radio. In. the
United States the Government has left it
to free and unfettered competition. Some
American newspapers have their own broad.
‘easting stations and. there is nothing to stop
the several hundreds of other American
stations from circulating news. Up to now
there has heen no serious development in

competitor.

this direction and the American Press has
not been affected by the competition
We are approaching the stage, however,

Sit ROBERT DONALD, G.BE,, LLD.
whose views are of  particul
the fact that he was for many years the ti
‘of a great London newspaper.
when the limitations placed upon radio
€annot well be maintained, The London

» LL.D.

newspaper with international atfiiations,
Its readers, or subscribers, will demand more
news, and if the Press and news agencies
put an embargo.on the supply, the B.B.C.
will be foreed to collect its own news of
all important events. Tt has been urged
that it is beyond the means and the capacity
of a broadcasting organization to collect
foreign news and that it must remain
dependent on existing agencies, That is not
the case, as broadcasting stations could
without difficulty arrange for an interchange
of news.

Supposing, however, that listeniers re
a larger service of news, it does not follow
that the Press will suffer to any appreciable
extent. A listener may be satished with
the results of spérting events, bith, as a
rule, he will want to read the news’ which
hhe has heard, just as an audience whiely
listens to a great oration wants to, see
it in print. The daily paper will be loft
With its headlines, with its pictures, with
its political articles, fiction and all its
general features, 10 siy nothing of its
nidvertisements.

There are practical difficulties in the Way.

distribution by broadcasting. Subscribers
will not want to listen to verbatim reports
ot. speeches, and’ when a Government
monopoly: begins to curtail <peeclies oF give
descriptive accounts of them, it cannot
escape the charge of impartiality. Publi
men who speak into a microphone at public
gatherings will be compelled to condense
their remarks—which will be ~ welcome
to those who see, nnd hy all who hear,
them.

The Story of Wireless
is the Story of Marconi

Early in, March, 1914, Senatore Marconi
communicated ssfully by _ Wireless
Telephony between Italian war-ships. On
the high seas consistently good reception was
obtained at a range of 44 miles, with the use

of only limited energy and ordinary receivers.

‘These experiments, in which radiotelephonic
communication was kept up for 12 hours on

end, conclusively established the practicability
of Wireless Telephony
In the latest development of | Wirgless—

Broadcasting—the name ‘Marconi fully
maintains its unchallenged lead. ‘The
Marconiphone is the Receiver on which you
can always rely implicitly, because it embodies
everything for which the name ‘ Marconi"
stands in Wireless,

LONDON HEARD AT THE CAPE,
EARLY every day news arrivist of fresh
wonders in long-distance wireless. The
latest comes by a Reuter message from Cape
‘Town, which states that the Landon Broad
castiny Station was picked up at Middle
(Cape Province), the programme having been
heard from 10.50 in the evening until 2.10 the
morning. Tt wax Inter reported that
Camps Bay, near Cape Town, had also picked
‘up items from the Lanudom Stati

Up to the time of wing to press, no official
confirmiation of this achievement’ had been
received by the B.ALC,, hub there seems no
reasott whatever to doubi its veracity.

‘Results like this open upp wonderful possibil
ties for tho listener, and it is probable that in a
very short time the civilized. world will
be his happy hunting ground.

‘The BARC. engineers are working hard wit
the idea of opening up new posiilities, and it
fs hoped that the Continent, and not’ merely
Paris, will very soon be brought into constant
toueh with: British listeners.

Developments during 1924 are certain to be
of an amazing character, and everyone with &
wireless set can congratulate himself that he has
many almost undveamed-of treats in store.

“La Bohéme.”

Saturday's Opera, described by Percy A. Scholes.

A BOHEMB means “Bohemia inthe
pootical sense. The plot is, for the most
part, drawn from Murger's novel, Seduea de
la Wie de Bohime, which relates inci
in the happy-go-lucky artiste’ quarter of Paris,
about a century ago. The music, by Puesini,
is lowing and tuneful and very’ Halian La
Bokéme is, in all countries, one of the most
Populae of Puccini's operas, ite skilful mixture
of humour and pathos providing probably one
of its strongest attractions.

Tt was first performed (in Turin) in 1800, and
was introduced to British audiences (at Man.
chester) by the. Carl Rora Company, the
following year. The following brief ‘account ix
intended ‘to be read in advance and” then
Tollowed as the opera proceeds,

ACT THE GARRET.

introduction, and the curtain rises on a garnet
in which live

‘© matter whether you are listening to Handel,
Bach, Mozartior any of the great masters of
the past, you cannot obtain the true interpre-

tation of their works by Radio unless you nse a Loud
Speaker capable of rendering loud and sonorous
passages as truthfully as delicate airs,
The ordinary Loud Speaker, for instance, using a
flat diaphragm, is compelled to compromise between
extremes of the harmonic scale—and, as everyone
will appreciate, a compromise can never be entirely
satisfactory,
The Brown, on the other hand, because it uses
entirely different principles, is remarkable for its
fidelity of tone. Its cone-shaped aluminium
diaphragm—as thin as paper—is anchored at its
exact centre to a vibrating reed. Thus extreme
sensitiveness is obtained with a complete absence
of distortion, Incidentally, these prineiples are used
in the famous A, type Headphones,

Ie isa significant fact thatthe first Loud Speaker ever taade in

this country for Wireless ues was designed by 5. G. Brown, Ld

who, tthe same time, originated the term “Loud Spesker.

‘The experience thus gained har calminated inthe prodactioa of

en Instrument without equal for purity and volume.

AT LAST!

Just as an imperfect mirror will give a
slight twist to your face or a pane of cheap
glass will distort a beautiful view, so wireless
often distorts the music, Generally it
bleaches the music and takes most of the
colour out of it,

This is a fault which has now been cured
by the Cosmos Radio Valve Sets. They
give you the music as it is in the concert
hall, in all its volume and variety. And so
it comes about that’as you listen to a
Cosmos Radio Set at home, the music
drives the miracle out of your mind and
the wonderful science of the thing is for-
gotten in its consummate artistry.
HEARING IS BELIEVING, — Before
choosing any wireless set, at least hear
the Cosmos. Then you will understand
why it is called the Musicians’ Set.
